The Starting Point of Scientific Research

Every psychological study starts with a question. A researcher notices something about human behaviour and wants to know why it happens, or whether one thing influences another. But noticing something and testing it scientifically are very different tasks. Before any data can be collected, a researcher must be precise: they must state exactly what they expect to find, define what they are measuring and ensure they have an appropriate group of participants. These steps are the foundation of scientific psychology.

Hypotheses

A hypothesis is a precise, testable prediction. It states in advance what the researcher expects to find. A hypothesis must be operationalised — meaning both the independent variable and the dependent variable must be defined in terms of how they will be measured, not described vaguely.

Compare these two predictions: “People who revise more will do better” versus “Participants who revise using flashcards for five hours will recall more words from a 20-word list than participants who reread their notes for five hours.” The second is a well-operationalised hypothesis because both conditions of the independent variable (flashcards vs rereading) and the dependent variable (words recalled from a 20-word list) are clearly defined and measurable.

Key Fact

A well-operationalised hypothesis states both conditions of the independent variable AND a clearly measurable dependent variable. Without operationalisation, a hypothesis cannot be properly tested, and mark schemes require both elements for full marks.

Null and Alternative Hypotheses

Every study involves two complementary hypotheses. The null hypothesis states that there is no difference or no relationship between the variables — any result found is due to chance. For example: “There will be no significant difference in word recall between participants who revise with flashcards and those who reread notes.”

The alternative hypothesis (also called the experimental hypothesis) states that there will be a difference or relationship — this is what the researcher expects to find. For example: “Participants who revise using flashcards will recall significantly more words from a 20-word list than those who reread their notes.”

Statistical testing after the study will determine whether the data allows the null hypothesis to be rejected. If results are ‘significant’ (unlikely to be due to chance), the null hypothesis is rejected and the alternative hypothesis is supported. Psychologists do not ‘prove’ their hypotheses; they provide evidence for or against them.

A independent variable (IV) is the one the researcher changes or manipulates. In the flashcard example, the IV is the revision method (flashcards vs rereading).

A dependent variable (DV) is what the researcher measures — the outcome. In the flashcard example, the DV is the number of words recalled from the 20-word list.

Extraneous variables are any other variables that could affect the DV that the researcher has not controlled. For example, if one group of participants had a higher baseline memory ability, that could explain any difference in word recall rather than the revision method. Controlling extraneous variables is essential to ensure results reflect the IV rather than something else.

Target Populations and Samples

A researcher almost never studies every member of a group they are interested in. Instead, they select a sample from the target population. The sample should be representative — it should reflect the characteristics of the target population as closely as possible so that conclusions can be generalised beyond the study itself.

Random sampling gives every member of the target population an equal chance of being selected. The researcher lists all members of the population and uses a random process (lottery, random number generator) to select participants. Strength: unbiased and representative. Weakness: requires a complete list of the population, which is often difficult to obtain, and non-responders may create a biased final sample.

Opportunity sampling selects whoever is available and willing to take part. A researcher standing at a university entrance and asking passers-by is using opportunity sampling. Strength: quick, easy and inexpensive. Weakness: biased towards people who are easily available at that time and place, so the sample may not be representative of the target population.

Systematic sampling selects every nth person from a list. For example, if there are 1,000 people in the population and you need 100 participants, you would select every 10th person. Strength: straightforward to carry out and reduces researcher bias. Weakness: may still be biased if the list has a pattern that makes every nth person systematically different.

Stratified sampling divides the population into subgroups (strata) based on relevant characteristics (e.g. age, gender) and then randomly selects participants from each stratum in proportion to their size in the full population. Strength: ensures the sample reflects the population structure, making it highly representative. Weakness: time-consuming and requires detailed knowledge of the population’s structure.

Key Fact

Four sampling methods: random (equal chance, unbiased but hard to obtain full list), opportunity (quick but biased towards available people), systematic (every nth person, straightforward but potential pattern bias), stratified (proportional subgroups, highly representative but time-consuming).

What Is Mental Health?

Mental health is not simply the absence of illness — it is a positive state. Good mental health involves being able to manage everyday challenges, form positive relationships and function effectively in daily life. Psychologists identify a range of characteristics that together describe what it means to be mentally healthy.

Key characteristics of good mental health include positive engagement with society — maintaining relationships and taking part in community life — and effective coping with challenges, such as managing stress, adapting to change and recovering from setbacks. A mentally healthy person does not feel overwhelmed by ordinary difficulties; they have the internal resources to work through them.

Key Fact

Good mental health includes two key features the spec identifies: positive engagement with society (maintaining relationships, contributing to community life) and effective coping with challenges (managing stress, adapting to change).

Cultural Variations in Beliefs About Mental Health

The way mental health and mental illness are understood is not universal — it varies significantly across cultures. Cultural variations affect whether certain experiences are seen as symptoms of illness or as spiritual, social or physical conditions.

In some cultures, what Western medicine classifies as a mental health condition may be attributed to supernatural causes, family conflicts or physical imbalances rather than psychological ones. This means that help-seeking behaviour, the willingness to disclose symptoms, and the type of treatment preferred all differ across cultural groups. Psychologists must be aware of this diversity to avoid imposing a narrow, culturally specific definition of normality.

How the Incidence of Mental Health Problems Changes Over Time

Reported rates of mental health problems have increased over recent decades. This change reflects a combination of genuine increases and changes in how mental health is perceived and discussed. Three main factors explain this trend.

Increased challenges of modern living, such as greater isolation, are one reason. Technology and changing social patterns have reduced face-to-face community contact for many people. Loneliness, financial pressures and work demands can contribute to poor mental health, and these stresses are widely seen as more prevalent than in previous generations.

Increased recognition of the nature of mental health problems is a second factor. Mental health conditions such as depression and anxiety are now better understood by both clinicians and the general public. As awareness grows, people are more likely to recognise their own experiences as symptoms and to seek help, leading to higher recorded rates even if the actual number of cases has not changed dramatically.

Lessening of social stigma is a third factor. Historically, admitting to a mental health problem could lead to discrimination, social exclusion or shame. As attitudes have shifted — driven by public campaigns, media representation and celebrities speaking openly — more people feel able to disclose difficulties, again increasing reported figures.

Effects of Significant Mental Health Problems on Individuals

Significant mental health problems affect every dimension of a person’s life. At an individual level, they can cause damage to relationships — making it difficult to maintain friendships, romantic partnerships or family bonds, often because of withdrawal, irritability or changes in behaviour. They create difficulties coping with day-to-day life, such as getting to work, managing finances or carrying out basic self-care. They can also have a negative impact on physical wellbeing: disrupted sleep, poor nutrition, reduced activity and neglect of medical needs are all associated with persistent mental health difficulties.

Key Fact

Individual effects: damage to relationships, difficulties coping with daily life, negative impact on physical wellbeing. Social effects: need for more social care, increased crime rates, implications for the economy.

Effects on Society

Mental health problems also have significant effects on wider society. There is an increased need for social care as more people require professional support, which places pressure on health and social services. Some research suggests links between untreated mental health conditions and increased crime rates, as individuals in crisis may act in ways they otherwise would not. The economic implications are also substantial: mental health problems are a major cause of lost productivity, absenteeism and long-term disability, costing the economy billions of pounds each year.

A note on language: the spec addresses these topics in clinical, educational terms. The purpose is to understand mental health as a field of study, not to label individuals. Describing mental health conditions accurately and without sensationalising them is a skill in itself — examiners reward precision and the ability to discuss these topics in a measured, factual way.
